extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers (readers of periodical essays); people seeking moral/practical advice on conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical-essay guidance on personal conduct: how to apply industry, evaluate hopes and schemes, use advice, and live in society. Emphasizes tests for rational plans, importance of diligent labour and social cooperation, and balance between hope and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of diligent labour
rubrics_metrics.description: He that will diligently labour, in whatever occupation, will deserve the sustenance which he obtains, and the protection which he enjoys; and may lie down every night with the pleasing consciousness of having contributed something to the happiness of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligent industry in any (even humble) occupation justifies one's livelihood and self-respect; idleness leads to no forward progress. Example passages argue that 'no man is without some quality' and that even small applied skills prevent one being 'useless or burthensome to the community.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as basis of respect
rubrics_metrics.description: No man can become venerable but by virtue, or contemptible but by wickedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social rank or station does not confer true dignity—virtue does. Likewise, apparent dignity can exist in low stations if accompanied by virtue. This is a moral standard for judging persons, not their outward condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply small abilities promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever he be that has but little in his power, should be in haste to do that little, lest he be confounded with him that can do nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act quickly on whatever limited capacity you possess; small consistent acts distinguish active contributors from the inert. The essay frames prompt application of small talents as an obligation against becoming a spectator amid universal labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of social cooperation and division of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive and to communicate assistance, constitutes the happiness of human life: man may, indeed, preserve his existence in solitude, but can enjoy it only in society... as one of a large community performing only his share of the common business, he gains leisure for intellectual pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society's interdependence (customs, manufactures, trades) supplies conveniences and frees individuals to pursue higher pleasures; the division of labour is praised as the foundation for material plenty and intellectual leisure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test schemes by external explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is true will bear to be related, whatever is rational will endure to be explained; but when we delight to brood in secret over future happiness... we are cheating ourselves by voluntary delusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical test for distinguishing reasonable hopes from fanciful ones: attempt to relate and explain the scheme to others. If a plan cannot be stated plainly without exposing its absurdity, it is likely a self-deception. The Tom Drowsy example illustrates how private confidence collapses under external scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break projects into manageable parts and act daily
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever can be completed in a year, is divisible into parts, of which each may be performed in the compass of a day; he, therefore, that has passed the day without attention to the task assigned him, may be certain, that the lapse of life has brought him no nearer to his object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical progress requires subdividing long tasks into daily actions and avoiding daily negligence. This is offered as a straightforward way to measure and ensure productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate hope as useful; excessive hope dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: These pleasures [of hope], like the rest, are lawful only in certain circumstances, and to certain degrees; they may be useful in a due subserviency to nobler purposes, but become dangerous and destructive when once they gain the ascendant in the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hope can invigorate and motivate when modestly held, but excessive or pervasive hope dulls faculties and leads to inaction or ruin. Use hope as a cordial in measured amounts, not as a substitute for effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine hope with effort; avoid passive expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The man of high courage and great abilities is apt to place too much confidence in himself... his mistaken ardour hurries him forward; and though, perhaps, he misses his end, he nevertheless obtains some collateral good... The drone of timidity presumes likewise to hope, but without ground and without consequence; the bliss with which he solaces his hours he always expects from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate active, risky hope that spurs useful action from passive hope that excuses inactivity: confidence coupled with exertion may produce benefits even when it fails, whereas idle hoping produces no gains and wastes life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of advice depends on manner and reception
rubrics_metrics.description: It has long been charged... that counsel and instruction are generally thrown away; they admit the efficacy of the medicine, but abhor the nauseousness of the vehicle... a patient listener is necessary to the accommodation of all those who desire to be confirmed in the opinion of their own wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice is valuable only when well-delivered and willingly received. The essay distinguishes moral/religious truths from prudential directions, notes that bad delivery ruins useful counsel, and that those who are talkative or conceited commonly reject instruction. Also warns that excessive reliance on advice (passive obedience) can cause missed opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced self-regard: confidence relative to tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion which a man entertains of himself ought to be distinguished, as it relates to persons or to things... To think highly of ourselves in comparison with others... must be always invidious and offensive; but to rate our powers high in proportion to things, and imagine ourselves equal to great undertakings... cannot with equal justice provoke censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages a measured self-confidence: be ambitious about what you can accomplish (relative to the task) but avoid arrogant social comparisons. Overconfidence can bring disgrace, yet reasonable confidence promotes large attempts and potential collateral good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality-check by seeking external judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: He soon discovered the impossibility of imposing upon others the notions by which he had so long imposed upon himself; which way soever he turned his thoughts, impossibility and absurdity arose in opposition on every side...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private conviction should be tested by attempting to persuade others; if external judgment exposes impossibility or absurdity, that reveals self-deception. Use public or critical scrutiny as a corrective to private fantasies.
